Summary:

In Drosophila melanogaster, ITP has functions in feeding, drinking, metabolism, excretion, and circadian rhythm. In the current study, the authors characterized and compared the expression of all three ITP isoforms (ITPa and ITPL1&2) in the CNS and peripheral tissues of Drosophila. An important finding is that they functionally characterized and identified Gyc76C as an ITPa receptor in Drosophila using both in vitro and in vivo approaches. In vitro, the authors nicely confirmed that the inhibitory function of recombinant Drosophila ITPa on MT secretion is Gyc76C-dependent (knockdown of Gyc76C specifically in two types of cells abolished the anti-diuretic action of Drosophila ITPa on renal tubules). They also confirmed that ITPa activates Gyc76C in a heterologous system. The authors used a combination of multiple approaches to investigate the roles of ITPa and Gyc76C on osmotic and metabolic homeostasis modulation in vivo. They revealed that ITPa signaling to renal tubules and fat body modulates osmotic and metabolic homeostasis via Gyc76C.

Furthermore, they tried to identify the upstream and downstream of ITP neurons in the nervous system by using connectomics and single-cell transcriptomic analysis. I found this interesting manuscript to be well-written and described. The findings in this study are valuable to help understand how ITP signals work on systemic homeostasis regulation. Both anatomical and single-cell transcriptome analysis here should be useful to many in the field.

Strengths:

The question (what receptors of ITPa in Drosophila) that this study tries to address is important. The authors ruled out the Bombyx ITPa receptor orthologs as potential candidates. They identified a novel ITP receptor by using phylogenetic, anatomical analysis, and both in vitro and in vivo approaches.

The authors exhibited detailed anatomical data of both ITP isoforms and Gyc76C (in the main and supplementary figures), which helped audiences understand the expression of the neurons studied in the manuscript.

They also performed connectomes and single-cell transcriptomics analyses to study the synaptic and peptidergic connectivity of ITP-expressing neurons. This provided more information for better understanding and further study of systemic homeostasis modulation.

Comments on revisions:

In the revised manuscript, the authors addressed all my concerns.

There is one more suggestion: The scale bar for fly and ovary images should be included in Figures 9, 10, and 12.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.97043.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97043.3.sa2)

The physiology and behaviour of animals are regulated by a huge variety of neuropeptide signalling systems. In this paper, the authors focus on the neuropeptide ion transport peptide (ITP), which was first identified and named on account of its effects on the locust hindgut (Audsley et al. 1992). Using Drosophila as an experimental model, the authors have mapped the expression of three different isoforms of ITP, all of which are encoded by the same gene.

The authors then investigated candidate receptors for isoforms of ITP. Firstly, Drosophila orthologs of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) that have been reported to act as receptors for ITPa or ITPL in the insect Bombyx mori were investigated. Importantly, the authors report that ITPa does not act as a ligand for the GPCRs TkR99D and PK2-R1. Therefore, the authors investigated other putative receptors for ITPs. Informed by a previously reported finding that ITP-type peptides cause an increase in cGMP levels in cells/tissues (Dircksen, 2009, Nagai et al., 2014), the authors investigated guanylyl cyclases as candidate receptors for ITPs. In particular, the authors suggest that Gyc76C may act as an ITP receptor in Drosophila. Evidence that Gyc76C may be involved in mediating effects of ITP in Bombyx was first reported by Nagai et al. (2014) and here the authors present further evidence, based on a proposed concordance in the phylogenetic distribution ITP-type neuropeptides and Gyc76C and experimental demonstration that ITPa causes dose-dependent stimulation of cGMP production in HEK cells expressing Gyc76C. Having performed detailed mapping of the expression of Gyc76C in Drosophila, the authors then investigated if Gyc76C knockdown affects the bioactivity of ITPa in Drosophila. The inhibitory effect of ITPa on leucokinin- and diuretic hormone-31-stimulated fluid secretion from Malpighian tubules was found to be abolished when expression of Gyc76C was knocked down in stellate cells and principal cells, respectively.

Having investigated the proposed mechanism of ITPa signalling in Drosophila, the authors then investigate its physiological roles at a systemic level. The authors present evidence that ITPa is released during desiccation and accordingly overexpression of ITPa increases survival when animals are subjected to desiccation. Furthermore, knockdown of Gyc76C in stellate or principal cells of Malphigian tubules decreases survival when animals are subject to desiccation. Furthermore, the relevance of the phenotypes observed to potential in vivo actions of ITPa is also explored and publicly available connectomic data and single-cell transcriptomic data are analysed to identify putative inputs and outputs of ITPa expressing neurons.

Strengths of this paper.

(1) The main strengths of this paper are:

(i) the detailed analysis of the expression and actions of ITP and the phenotypic consequences of over-expression of ITPa in Drosophila.

(ii). the detailed analysis of the expression of Gyc76C and the phenotypic consequences of knockdown of Gyc76C expression in Drosophila.

(iii). the experimental demonstration that ITPa causes dose-dependent stimulation of cGMP production in HEK cells expressing Gyc76C, providing biochemical evidence that the effects of ITPa in Drosophila are, at least in part, mediated by Gyc76C.

(2) Furthermore, the paper is generally well written and the figures are of good quality.

Weaknesses of this paper.

A weakness of this paper is the phylogenetic analysis to investigate if there is correspondence in the phylogenetic distribution of ITP-type and Gyc76C-type genes/proteins. Unfortunately, the evidence presented is rather limited in scope. Essentially, the authors report that they only found ITP-type and Gyc76C-type genes/proteins in protostomes, but not in deuterostomes. What is needed is a more fine-grained analysis at the species level within the protostomes. However, I recognise that such a detailed analysis may extend beyond the scope of this paper, which is already rich in data.

results.result: The Drosophila ITP gene generates three distinct peptide isoforms through alternative splicing: ITPa (a C-terminally amidated 73 amino acid neuropeptide), ITPL1, and ITPL2 (both non-amidated with alternate, extended C-termini).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11, and C12 are directly supported by the gene structure analysis shown in Figure 1A, which clearly depicts the transcript variants and their corresponding peptide products. The structural characterization is consistent with established molecular biology principles.

results.result: ITPa is expressed in specific neuronal populations in the brain and VNC, including seven bilateral pairs of brain neurons (L-NSCITP, LNdITP, 5th-LNv, and L-NSCDH31) and abdominal ganglion efferent neurons (iag) in the VNC. These neurons co-express multiple neuropeptides including tachykinin, sNPF, LK, DH31, Ast-A, and CCAP.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 are well-supported by comprehensive immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1 and 2, combined with citations to previous literature. The co-expression patterns are clearly demonstrated through multi-label immunofluorescence experiments.

results.result: ITP isoforms show widespread expression in peripheral tissues beyond the nervous system. ITPL2 is broadly expressed in heart muscles, pericardial nephrocytes, midgut, ureter, and trachea, while ITPa and ITPL1 expression is more restricted to peripheral neurons innervating the heart and rectum.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 are supported by both single-nucleus transcriptome analysis (Fly Cell Atlas data, Figures 3A-D) and anatomical mapping using GAL4 drivers and immunolabeling (Figures 3E-R). The convergence of transcriptomic and anatomical evidence provides strong support.

results.result: ITP/CHH/MIH peptides are evolutionarily conserved across protostomian invertebrates (arthropods, nematodes, tardigrades, priapulid worms, and mollusks) but absent from deuterostomes and vertebrates. The six cysteine residues and adjacent amino acids are highly conserved across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C13 are supported by comprehensive phylogenetic analysis using BLAST and HMM-based searches, with sequence alignments shown in Figure 4A. The phyletic distribution pattern is clearly demonstrated, though the absence from deuterostomes could benefit from more explicit negative search results.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis of membrane guanylate cyclase receptors identified Gyc76C as a candidate ITPa receptor based on co-evolution with ITP peptides. Gyc76C belongs to a clade of receptors restricted to protostomian invertebrates, matching the phyletic distribution of ITP.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B with appropriate bootstrap values (>200 from 500 replicates). The phylogenetic-driven approach is sound, though C4's designation of Gyc76C as a "bona fide" receptor requires additional functional validation beyond phylogenetics alone.

results.result: The Bombyx ITPa/ITPL receptor orthologs (PK2-R1, TkR99D, and CG30340) are not expressed in Drosophila rectal pad epithelial cells and recombinant ITPa failed to activate TkR99D and PK2-R1 in heterologous CHO-K1 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by GAL4 driver expression analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and functional assays in CHO-K1 cells with appropriate positive controls (tachykinin 1 and pyrokinin 2). This effectively rules out these GPCRs as ITPa receptors in the osmoregulatory context.

results.result: Gyc76C is highly expressed in tissues associated with osmoregulation (renal tubules, rectum) and metabolic homeostasis (fat body), as well as in neurons throughout the brain and VNC, clock neurons, and corpora allata. Expression patterns show sex-specific differences in insulin-producing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C42 are comprehensively supported by multiple lines of evidence including single-nucleus sequencing data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), GAL4 driver expression patterns (Figure 5), and immunohistochemistry. The convergence of ITPa-immunolabeled axon terminations with Gyc76C expression (C37) provides strong anatomical support for a functional relationship.

results.result: Recombinant ITPa does not affect basal secretion by unstimulated renal tubules but inhibits both leucokinin (LK)-stimulated and diuretic hormone 31 (DH31)-stimulated fluid secretion in ex vivo Ramsay assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by Ramsay assay data shown in Figures 6B-D with appropriate statistical analysis (unpaired t-tests, p<0.05 and p<0.0001). The differential effect on stimulated versus unstimulated tubules is clearly demonstrated, confirming ITPa's anti-diuretic role.

results.result: Genetic knockdown of Gyc76C in either stellate cells (using c724-GAL4) or principal cells (using uro-GAL4) of renal tubules abolishes the anti-diuretic action of ITPa in LK-stimulated and DH31-stimulated tubules, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are strongly supported by Ramsay assay data with genetic manipulation (Figures 6E-F) using appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA with Tukey's test). The cell-type-specific knockdown experiments provide compelling evidence that Gyc76C mediates ITPa's anti-diuretic effects. However, the observation that ITPa alone promotes secretion in knockdown tubules (mentioned in text) suggests additional complexity.

results.result: HEK293T cells expressing Gyc76C and the cGMP biosensor Green cGull show dose-dependent increases in fluorescence (34%, 88.7%, and 111.4% at 50, 250, and 500 nM ITPa, respectively) following ITPa treatment, while control cells show no clear dose-dependent response.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by live-cell imaging data (Figures 7B-G) with appropriate controls and statistical analysis (nonparametric one-way ANOVA with Dunn's test, p<0.05 and p<0.0001). Post-hoc immunostaining confirmed receptor expression. The dose-dependent response in Gyc76C-expressing cells versus controls provides strong evidence for ITPa-Gyc76C signaling via cGMP.

results.result: During desiccation, L-NSCITP neurons show increased activity (measured by CaLexA reporter) and reduced ITPa immunofluorescence (indicating peptide release) in both males and females. Both activity and peptide levels return to normal upon rehydration.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by CaLexA reporter assays and ITPa immunofluorescence measurements (Figure 8) with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's test, p<0.05 to p<0.0001). The reversibility upon rehydration strengthens the conclusion that ITPa release is dynamically regulated by hydration state.

results.result: ITP knockdown in ITP-RC neurons results in reduced desiccation tolerance, water retention, and starvation survival, along with decreased circulating glucose and lipid stores (but unaltered glycogen), smaller ovaries, increased feeding, and disrupted preference for nutritive sugars during starvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C63 are supported by comprehensive phenotypic analysis (Figure 9) using adult-specific knockdown (ITP-RC-GAL4TS) with appropriate controls and statistical tests. The convergent phenotypes across multiple assays provide strong evidence for ITP's role in osmotic and metabolic homeostasis. However, the RNAi targets all ITP isoforms, so effects cannot be attributed specifically to ITPa (acknowledged by authors).

results.result: ITPa overexpression in ITP-RC neurons produces phenotypes largely opposite to ITP knockdown: improved desiccation tolerance, increased water content, enhanced starvation survival, reduced glucose levels, increased lipid levels, altered sugar preference, and larger ovaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are supported by comprehensive phenotypic analysis (Figure 10) with appropriate controls and statistical tests (Log-rank test for survival, one-way ANOVA for other measures). The opposite phenotypes compared to knockdown provide strong complementary evidence for ITPa's functions. The specificity to ITPa (versus other ITP isoforms) is better established here than in knockdown experiments.

results.result: Gyc76C knockdown in renal tubules reduces desiccation tolerance regardless of cell type (principal or stellate), but differentially affects salt stress tolerance (increased survival in principal cells, decreased in stellate cells) and increases chill-coma recovery time in both cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by stress tolerance assays (Figure 11) with cell-type-specific knockdown using uro-GAL4 and c724-GAL4. The differential effects on salt stress (C72-C73) are intriguing but lack mechanistic explanation. The chill-coma results support a role in ionic homeostasis.

results.result: Fat body-specific Gyc76C knockdown causes severe metabolic defects including drastically reduced starvation tolerance, lower glucose and lipid levels, increased feeding, altered food preferences, smaller ovaries, increased defecation, lower water content, reduced DILP2 peptide levels, and decreased daytime locomotor activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C86 are supported by extensive phenotypic characterization (Figure 12) using yolk-GAL4 for fat body-specific knockdown, with validation using a second RNAi line (Figure 12—figure supplement 1). The severe and pleiotropic phenotypes demonstrate the critical role of ITPa-Gyc76C signaling in the fat body. The reduced DILP2 levels (C84) suggest crosstalk with insulin signaling.

results.result: Connectomic analysis reveals that LNdITP and 5th-LNv clock neurons have extensive synaptic connections with diverse neuron types and are upstream of DH31-expressing neurons, while L-NSCITP form few synaptic connections within the brain. LNdITP receive indirect inputs from thermo/hygrosensory neurons, and L-NSCITP output to osmoregulatory hormone-producing neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by comprehensive connectomic analysis using the FlyWire adult brain connectome (Figure 13) with a threshold of five synapses for significant connections. The differential connectivity patterns between neuron types are clearly demonstrated. However, the functional significance of these connections requires experimental validation.

results.result: Single-cell transcriptome analysis reveals that ITP neurons express diverse neuromodulator receptors, with Dop2R (dopamine receptor) highly expressed in all ITP neuron subtypes, brain ITP neurons extensively modulated by neuropeptides regulating osmotic and metabolic homeostasis, and high neurotransmitter receptor expression in all ITP neurons except L-NSCITP.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by single-cell transcriptome analysis from published datasets (Figure 13H-J, Figure 13—figure supplement 2). The receptor expression patterns provide insights into potential regulatory mechanisms, though functional validation is needed. The lack of neurotransmitter receptors in L-NSCITP (C95) is consistent with their sparse synaptic connectivity (C91).

results.result: The multifunctional ITP signaling system in Drosophila shows functional parallels to mammalian atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) signaling, including roles in regulating water/sodium excretion by kidney/renal tubules and lipid metabolism in adipocytes/fat body.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 represent comparative analysis supported by citations to ANP literature and the experimental data from this study. The functional parallels are valid, though C97 is general knowledge rather than a novel finding. The comparison provides useful evolutionary context but is somewhat speculative regarding convergent evolution.

results.result: ITP and Gyc76C are absent in mammals, and no orthologs of ANP have been discovered in invertebrates, suggesting independent evolution of these functionally analogous signaling systems.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study (Figure 4) and established knowledge. However, the absence of ANP orthologs in invertebrates could be more rigorously demonstrated with explicit negative search results rather than relying on lack of prior discovery.

results.result: ITPa-producing neurons are activated and release ITPa during dehydration.
results.evaluation: Claim C2 is directly supported by the experimental data in Figure 8, which shows increased neuronal activity (CaLexA reporter) and reduced ITPa immunofluorescence (indicating release) during desiccation. This claim is already covered in the result grouping C50-C53 but warrants separate mention as a key finding stated in the abstract.

results.result: Recombinant Drosophila ITPa inhibits diuretic peptide-induced renal tubule secretion ex vivo, confirming its role as an anti-diuretic hormone.
results.evaluation: Claim C3 is supported by Ramsay assay data (Figures 6C-D) showing inhibition of both LK- and DH31-stimulated secretion. This claim is already covered in the result grouping C43-C45 but is highlighted separately as a major conclusion stated in the abstract.

results.result: Gyc76C is highly expressed in larval and adult tissues associated with osmoregulation (renal tubules and rectum) and metabolic homeostasis (fat body).
results.evaluation: Claim C5 is supported by extensive anatomical mapping shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. This claim is already covered in the result grouping C34-C42 but is highlighted separately as a major finding stated in the abstract.

results.result: Knockdown of Gyc76C in renal tubules impacts tolerance to osmotic and ionic stresses.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 is supported by stress tolerance assays shown in Figure 11. This claim is already covered in the result grouping C71-C74 but is highlighted separately as a major finding stated in the abstract.

results.result: Knockdown of Gyc76C in the fat body impacts feeding, nutrient homeostasis, and associated behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is supported by comprehensive phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 12. This claim is already covered in the result grouping C75-C86 but is highlighted separately as a major finding stated in the abstract.

results.result: The Drosophila ITP gene generates three peptide isoforms: ITPa (C-terminally amidated, 73 amino acids), ITPL1, and ITPL2 (both non-amidated with extended C-termini), as shown by gene structure analysis and transcript variants.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the characterization of ITP isoforms without question. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'characterized and compared the expression of all three ITP isoforms' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors have mapped the expression of three different isoforms of ITP.' No concerns were raised about this structural characterization.

results.result: Gyc76C is identified as the Drosophila ITPa receptor through phylogenetic analysis showing two protostome-specific membrane guanylyl cyclase clades, with Gyc76C more highly expressed than Gyc32E in Malpighian tubules. Recombinant ITPa failed to activate the previously reported Bombyx receptors TkR99D and PK2-R1 in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: All reviewers strongly support this identification. Reviewer 1 states 'they functionally characterized and identified Gyc76C as an ITPa receptor in Drosophila using both in vitro and in vivo approaches.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'the authors report that ITPa does not act as a ligand for the GPCRs TkR99D and PK2-R1' and notes the phylogenetic evidence. Reviewer 3 states 'the evidence presented in favor of this model is very strong as it combines multiple approaches.'

results.result: Recombinant Drosophila ITPa inhibits diuretic peptide-induced renal tubule secretion ex vivo, specifically inhibiting both LK-stimulated secretion (stellate cells) and DH31-stimulated secretion (principal cells), but does not affect unstimulated tubules.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously accept the anti-diuretic function. Reviewer 2 states 'The inhibitory effect of ITPa on leucokinin- and diuretic hormone-31-stimulated fluid secretion from Malpighian tubules was found to be abolished when expression of Gyc76C was knocked down.' Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'nicely confirmed that the inhibitory function of recombinant Drosophila ITPa on MT secretion is Gyc76C-dependent.'

results.result: Knockdown of Gyc76C in stellate cells abolished the anti-diuretic action of ITPa in LK-stimulated tubules, and knockdown in principal cells abolished the anti-diuretic action in DH31-stimulated tubules, demonstrating cell-type-specific receptor function.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept this genetic validation. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'knockdown of Gyc76C specifically in two types of cells abolished the anti-diuretic action of Drosophila ITPa on renal tubules.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'The inhibitory effect of ITPa...was found to be abolished when expression of Gyc76C was knocked down in stellate cells and principal cells, respectively.'

results.result: HEK293T cells expressing Gyc76C and Green cGull exhibited dose-dependent increases in fluorescence (34%, 88.7%, and 111.4% at 50, 250, and 500 nM ITPa), indicating cGMP production, while control cells showed no clear dose-dependent response.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this biochemical evidence. Reviewer 2 highlights 'the experimental demonstration that ITPa causes dose-dependent stimulation of cGMP production in HEK cells expressing Gyc76C, providing biochemical evidence that the effects of ITPa in Drosophila are, at least in part, mediated by Gyc76C' as a key strength. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'confirmed that ITPa activates Gyc76C in a heterologous system.'

results.result: Gyc76C is highly expressed in tissues associated with osmoregulation (renal tubules, rectum including rectal papillae) and metabolic homeostasis (fat body), with convergence of ITPa-immunolabeled axon terminations and Gyc76C expression in the anterior midgut and rectal papillae.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the anatomical mapping. Reviewer 1 states 'The authors exhibited detailed anatomical data of both ITP isoforms and Gyc76C (in the main and supplementary figures), which helped audiences understand the expression of the neurons studied.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the detailed analysis of the expression of Gyc76C' as a strength. No concerns were raised about the expression patterns.

results.result: ITPa-producing neurons (L-NSCITP) are activated during dehydration (shown by increased CaLexA reporter fluorescence) and release ITPa (shown by reduced ITPa immunofluorescence), with both measures returning to normal levels upon rehydration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this physiological activation evidence. Reviewer 2 states 'The authors present evidence that ITPa is released during desiccation and accordingly overexpression of ITPa increases survival when animals are subjected to desiccation.' No concerns were raised about the CaLexA or immunofluorescence data demonstrating neuronal activation and peptide release.

results.result: ITP knockdown resulted in reduced desiccation tolerance, reduced water retention, and increased defecation, while ITPa overexpression improved desiccation tolerance, increased body water content, and caused bloated abdomens.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously support these osmoregulatory phenotypes. Reviewer 2 states 'overexpression of ITPa increases survival when animals are subjected to desiccation' and 'knockdown of Gyc76C in stellate or principal cells of Malpighian tubules decreases survival when animals are subject to desiccation.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the evidence presented in favor of this model is very strong.'

results.result: Knockdown of Gyc76C in renal tubules impacts tolerance to osmotic and ionic stresses: both principal and stellate cell knockdown reduced desiccation tolerance and increased chill-coma recovery time, but had opposite effects on salt stress (principal cell knockdown increased survival, stellate cell knockdown decreased survival).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these stress tolerance phenotypes. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'knockdown of Gyc76C in stellate or principal cells of Malpighian tubules decreases survival when animals are subject to desiccation.' The differential effects on salt stress are presented as data without reviewer challenge, suggesting acceptance of the cell-type-specific functional differences.

results.result: Knockdown of Gyc76C in the fat body impacts metabolic homeostasis: reduced starvation tolerance, lower glucose and lipids (but normal glycogen), increased feeding, altered food preferences, smaller ovaries, increased defecation, lower water content, reduced DILP2 levels, and reduced daytime activity. ITP knockdown showed similar metabolic phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the comprehensive metabolic phenotyping. Reviewer 1 states 'They revealed that ITPa signaling to renal tubules and fat body modulates osmotic and metabolic homeostasis via Gyc76C.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the detailed analysis of...the phenotypic consequences of knockdown of Gyc76C expression in Drosophila' as a strength. The extensive metabolic data are not questioned.

results.result: ITPa overexpression led to improved starvation survival, reduced glucose levels, increased lipid levels, defects in nutritive versus non-nutritive sugar preference, and larger ovaries.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the overexpression phenotypes as complementary to knockdown data. Reviewer 2 states 'flies with ITPa overexpression survive longer under starvation' and notes the overall evidence is strong. No concerns were raised about these gain-of-function experiments.

results.result: Detailed anatomical mapping shows ITPa is localized in at least seven bilateral pairs of brain neurons (including L-NSCITP that co-express tachykinin, sNPF, and LK; and L-NSCDH31 that co-express DH31), sparse VNC expression in iag neurons (co-expressing Ast-A and CCAP), and widespread peripheral expression in trachea, Malpighian tubules, heart, fat body, and gut. All ITPa brain neurons co-express ITPL1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support the anatomical characterization. Reviewer 1 states 'The authors exhibited detailed anatomical data of both ITP isoforms and Gyc76C (in the main and supplementary figures), which helped audiences understand the expression of the neurons studied in the manuscript.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the detailed analysis of the expression and actions of ITP' as a strength. The comprehensive mapping is treated as a valuable contribution.

results.result: Gyc76C is broadly expressed in neurons throughout the brain and VNC, in glia clock cells and subsets of dorsal clock neurons, not in male IPCs but in a subset of female IPCs, not in AKH-producing cells, and in the corpora allata.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the detailed Gyc76C expression mapping. Reviewer 2 highlights 'the detailed analysis of the expression of Gyc76C' as a strength. The sex-specific expression patterns and absence from certain endocrine cells are presented without reviewer challenge.

results.result: Connectomics analysis reveals that LNdITP and 5th-LNv clock neurons display numerous synapses and connect to a broad range of neurons, including being upstream of DH31-expressing NSC, with LNdITP receiving indirect inputs from VP1l thermo/hygrosensory neurons. In contrast, L-NSCITP form few synaptic connections but output onto other NSC subtypes secreting osmoregulatory hormones like DH31 and CRZ.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the connectomics data. Reviewer 1 states 'They also performed connectomes and single-cell transcriptomics analyses to study the synaptic and peptidergic connectivity of ITP-expressing neurons. This provided more information for better understanding and further study of systemic homeostasis modulation.' The connectivity patterns are not questioned.

results.result: Single-cell transcriptome analysis shows the dopamine receptor Dop2R is highly expressed in all ITP neuron subtypes, brain ITP neurons are extensively modulated by neuropeptides regulating osmotic and metabolic homeostasis, and all ITP neurons except L-NSCITP express high levels of neurotransmitter receptors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support the transcriptomic characterization. Reviewer 1 notes 'Both anatomical and single-cell transcriptome analysis here should be useful to many in the field.' The receptor expression patterns are presented as valuable context without reviewer challenge.

results.result: The candidate Drosophila receptors PK2-R1, TkR99D, and CG30340 (orthologs of Bombyx ITP receptors) are not expressed in rectal pad epithelial cells, and recombinant ITPa failed to activate TkR99D and PK2-R1 in heterologous CHO-K1 cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this negative result as important for ruling out alternative receptors. Reviewer 2 states 'Importantly, the authors report that ITPa does not act as a ligand for the GPCRs TkR99D and PK2-R1' and notes this led to investigation of guanylyl cyclases. Reviewer 1 confirms 'The authors ruled out the Bombyx ITPa receptor orthologs as potential candidates.'

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis shows ITP/CHH/MIH-like genes are found in arthropods, nematodes, tardigrades, priapulid worms, and mollusks, with six conserved cysteines and adjacent residues highly conserved. ITP appears restricted to protostomian invertebrates without orthologs in deuterostomes and vertebrates.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 identifies a weakness: 'the phylogenetic analysis to investigate if there is correspondence in the phylogenetic distribution of ITP-type and Gyc76C-type genes/proteins. Unfortunately, the evidence presented is rather limited in scope...What is needed is a more fine-grained analysis at the species level within the protostomes.' However, the reviewer acknowledges 'such a detailed analysis may extend beyond the scope of this paper.' The basic phylogenetic distribution is accepted but noted as incomplete.

results.result: Background claims about ITP function and homology: ITP was first identified in locust as an anti-diuretic hormone, influences feeding/drinking/metabolism/excretion in Drosophila, has a role in the circadian clock, is homologous to crustacean CHH/MIH, is produced by interneurons and NSC in the brain and VNC, and Bombyx ITP isoforms activate GPCR receptors for pyrokinin and tachykinin.
results.evaluation: These are established background facts supported by citations. Reviewers accept them without question as they provide context for the current study. Reviewer 2 notes 'the neuropeptide ion transport peptide (ITP), which was first identified and named on account of its effects on the locust hindgut.'

results.result: The multifunctional ITP signaling characterized here is reminiscent of mammalian ANP signaling: ANP is secreted from cardiac muscle to regulate sodium and water excretion by the kidney and targets white adipocytes to affect lipid metabolism, similar to ITPa actions on the Drosophila fat body. However, ITP and Gyc76C are absent in mammals and no ANP orthologs exist in invertebrates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this comparative discussion. Reviewer 3 notes 'these findings represent an important contribution to the field of insect neuropeptides and neurohormones and has strong relevance for other animals.' The parallel to ANP is presented as interpretive context without challenge.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on C1, C11, C12. Both evaluations support the structural characterization of ITP isoforms and transcript variants shown in Figure 1A without any concerns.

Perfect agreement on C27, C28. Both evaluations strongly support the negative result ruling out TkR99D and PK2-R1 as ITPa receptors, viewing this as important evidence that led to identification of Gyc76C.
Perfect agreement on C46, C47. Both evaluations support the genetic validation showing Gyc76C knockdown in stellate and principal cells abolishes ITPa's anti-diuretic effects.

Perfect agreement on C48, C49. Both evaluations strongly support the biochemical evidence showing ITPa stimulates cGMP production in Gyc76C-expressing cells, with peer reviewers highlighting this as a key strength.
Perfect agreement on C87-C92. Both evaluations accept the connectomics analysis showing differential synaptic connectivity patterns between ITP neuron types without concerns.
Perfect agreement on C93-C95. Both evaluations support the single-cell transcriptome analysis of receptor expression patterns in ITP neurons, viewing it as valuable context.
Strong agreement on C50-C53 (C2 also in peer R7). Both evaluations support the CaLexA and immunofluorescence evidence showing ITPa release during desiccation, with reversibility upon rehydration.
Strong agreement on C71-C74 (C6 also in peer R9). Both evaluations accept the stress tolerance phenotypes from cell-type-specific Gyc76C knockdown, including differential salt stress effects.
Strong agreement on C43-C45 (C3 also in peer R3). Both evaluations support the Ramsay assay data showing ITPa's anti-diuretic function and its dependence on Gyc76C.

Strong agreement on C32-C33, C4 (C28, C34 also in peer R2). Both evaluations support Gyc76C identification as ITPa receptor through phylogenetic and functional evidence. OpenEval notes C4 requires additional functional validation beyond phylogenetics; peer reviewers emphasize the strength of combined approaches.

Partial agreement on C29-C31 (C13 also in OpenEval R4). OpenEval supports the phylogenetic distribution but notes absence from deuterostomes could benefit from more explicit negative results. Peer reviewer identifies this as UNCERTAIN, requesting more fine-grained species-level analysis within protostomes, though acknowledging it may be beyond scope.

Agreement on C96-C98 (C99 in both). Both evaluations accept the comparative analysis with ANP as valid interpretive context, though OpenEval notes C97 is general knowledge and the convergent evolution claim is somewhat speculative.

Strong agreement on C17-C22 (C23-C26 also in peer R12). Both evaluations support the comprehensive immunohistochemistry and anatomical mapping of ITP isoforms, viewing the detailed data as valuable for the field.
Strong agreement on C23-C26 (C17-C22 also in peer R12). Both evaluations support the convergence of single-nucleus transcriptome and anatomical mapping evidence for ITP expression patterns.

Strong agreement on C35-C37 (C34-C42 in OpenEval R7, C5 in peer R6). Both evaluations accept the detailed anatomical mapping of Gyc76C expression and convergence with ITPa-immunolabeled axon terminations.
Strong agreement on C38-C42. Both evaluations support the detailed Gyc76C expression mapping including sex-specific patterns and absence from certain endocrine cells.

Strong agreement on C75-C86 (C7, C57-C63 overlap with peer R10). Both evaluations support the comprehensive metabolic phenotyping from fat body-specific Gyc76C knockdown, viewing the pleiotropic effects as demonstrating critical signaling role.

Strong agreement on C54-C56 (C57-C63 also in OpenEval R12, C64-C65 in peer R8). Both evaluations support the osmoregulatory phenotypes from ITP knockdown and overexpression, though OpenEval notes RNAi affects all isoforms.
Strong agreement on C66-C70. Both evaluations support the ITPa overexpression phenotypes as complementary evidence, with opposite effects compared to knockdown providing strong validation.

Strong agreement on C57-C63 (C54-C63 in OpenEval R12, broader metabolic claims in peer R10). Both evaluations accept the comprehensive phenotypic characterization showing ITPa's role in osmotic and metabolic homeostasis.
Strong agreement on C64-C65 (C64-C70 in OpenEval R13, C54-C56, C64-C65 in peer R8). Both evaluations support the desiccation survival phenotypes from ITPa overexpression.
Agreement on C99. Both evaluations support the claim about ANP absence in invertebrates, though OpenEval notes this could be more rigorously demonstrated with explicit negative search results.

Agreement on C2. Both evaluations support the evidence for ITPa release during desiccation. OpenEval notes this is a key abstract finding already covered in R11; peer review accepts it as part of physiological activation evidence.

Agreement on C3. Both evaluations support the anti-diuretic function claim. OpenEval notes this abstract claim is already covered in R8; peer reviewers unanimously accept the inhibitory effect on tubule secretion.
Agreement on C5. Both evaluations support the anatomical mapping claim. OpenEval notes this abstract finding is covered in R7; peer reviewers accept the detailed expression data as valuable.
Agreement on C6. Both evaluations support the stress tolerance claim. OpenEval notes this abstract finding is covered in R14; peer reviewers accept the cell-type-specific knockdown effects.
Agreement on C7. Both evaluations support the fat body signaling claim. OpenEval notes this abstract finding is covered in R15; peer reviewers accept the comprehensive metabolic phenotyping.

Minimal overlap on C13. OpenEval R4 addresses phylogenetic distribution (C29-C31, C13); peer R18 addresses background facts (C8-C16) that are accepted as established context. Limited direct comparison possible.
